Subject: RFP follow-up: high-level segmentation and attack hypotheses

Kim,

Thanks for the quick intro call this morning. As part of our security review for the inference platform RFP, our architecture team asked for a focused write-up that shows:

- High-level deployment topology for a multi-tenant hosted model serving environment (control plane vs data plane).
- Tenant boundary controls and how we prevent noisy-neighbor and data leakage scenarios.
- Concrete attack hypotheses you considered and mitigations (eg: token provenance spoofing, KV cache poisoning, lateral movement from sidecars).

If possible, please attach a diagram and a short bulleted threat summary. We need this for our security review packet by EOD Friday.

Subject: Re: RFP follow-up: high-level segmentation and attack hypotheses

Tom —

Appreciate the clarity. I attached a compact diagram (PDF + PNG) and a short threat summary below. This response is intended to be concise for your packet; happy to expand any section with deeper artefacts (config snippets, firewall rules, evidentiary logs).

Attachment: vanguard_segmentation_diagram_v1.png (diagram showing control plane, per-tenant inference pools, sidecar boundary, bastion and egress paths)
Attachment: tenant_boundary_evidence_20280703.pdf (controls list and policy excerpts)

Key points (short):
- Logical separation: control plane lives in a customer-managed VPC when deployed privately; hosted option uses isolated control namespaces per customer with per-tenant encryption keys.
- Data plane tenancy: inference workloads run in dedicated tenant pools by default for regulated customers; shared pools require mandatory mTLS + token provenance checks + per-request tenant assertion headers.
- Sidecar model: request routing and KV cache handled by an L7 sidecar with mTLS pinned to runtime identity; sidecars are ephemeral and constrained with seccomp + capability drops.
- KV cache integrity: write paths to shared caches require signed nonce tokens from the runtime and are scrubbed by prefix validation; read-only cache entries are bounded by TTLs and tenant tags.
- Egress control: enforced using per-tenant egress policies and NAT gateways; sensitive customers can opt for no-internet egress and customer-managed gateways.

Attack hypotheses (top 3) and mitigations (one-line each):
1) Token provenance spoofing — Mitigation: short-lived signed bearer tokens issued by control plane KMS; runtime validates signature + nonce + tenant id on every request.
2) KV cache poisoning (poisoned prefix leading to model prompt injection) — Mitigation: cache write ACLs require a signed authorizer token + content fingerprinting; critical prompts are client-side hashed and verified.
3) Lateral movement via sidecar compromise — Mitigation: sidecars run in hardened containers with mandatory mTLS to node agent, no host network, and eBPF sandboxing for syscalls where required.

I'll loop Marcus with the implementation specifics if you want platform-level configs.

Best,

Subject: Vanguard - segmentation design and attack hypotheses (packet attached)

Tom / Elena —

Thanks for the request and the early review. We've consolidated a short packet attached to this thread. Highlights below and attachments are included for your security review packet:

Attachments: vanguard_segmentation_diagram_v1.png, tenant_boundary_evidence_20280703.pdf

Executive summary (two bullets):
- Redwood’s hosted inference topology enforces tenant separation through a combination of tenancy-aware routing, cryptographic token provenance, and optional dedicated inference pools for high-regulation customers.
- Our hardening and detection controls focus on preventing integrity attacks (cache poisoning, token spoofing) and limiting lateral movement via sidecar and host-level constraints.

Selected technical notes (short):
- Control plane isolation (private deployments): control plane components can be deployed into customer-managed subnets with restricted egress and maintenance windows. Patch orchestration runs via an agent that authenticates to the customer's KMS and is visible in the customer audit logs.
- Token model: tokens are signed with a customer-key where requested; signature validation includes tenant id, nonce, TTL and scope. Tokens are rejected if the token-origin header does not match the runtime identity observed in the mTLS cert.
- Sidecar constraints: sidecars use ephemeral certs rotated every 6 hours; all sidecar-to-node communication requires mutual TLS and is mediated by a node-level agent that enforces network policies.
- KV cache guidance: recommend per-tenant keyspace prefixes and strict prefix write ACLs; for sensitive customers we offer per-tenant dedicated cache clusters.

Top attack hypotheses we provided (abridged):
- Privileged token replay/spoof: mitigated by short TTLs, nonces & signature checks.
- Cache poisoning leading to prompt manipulation: mitigated via write ACLs, content fingerprints, and optional per-tenant caches.
- Sidecar compromise and lateral movement: mitigated via container hardening, eBPF syscall filters, and segmented networking that prevents east-west access to unrelated tenants.

What we included: diagram PNG, a two-page evidence PDF (policy extracts, sample logs, runtime hardening checklist), and links to a console trace showing token validation flows.

If Vanguard needs a live walkthrough (15–30 minutes) of the Console + a short threat-hypothesis Q&A, we can run that tomorrow morning — suggest 30-min slot at 10:00am PT.

Best regards,
Kimberly Park
